data.title: Distributed System
data.tagline: A distributed system uses multiple computing nodes that coordinate over a network to achieve a system goal.
data.learningOutcome: You can decide when troubleshooting must account for network communication and partial failure, and identify where a request stopped.
data.description: During checkout, order, inventory, and payment services may run separately and exchange requests and results over a network. An inventory timeout does not mean every service stopped, so the system must handle partial failure. Multiple threads in one process share process resources and are not automatically a distributed system; the important boundary is network communication and independent failure.

learning.assumes: You know a backend feature can be split across multiple services or runtime nodes.
learning.outcome: You can decide when troubleshooting must account for network communication and partial failure, and identify where a request stopped.

distinctions.label: Multi-Instance
distinctions.explanation: Multi-Instance Deployment runs identical replicas of the same service for load distribution; a Distributed System coordinates distinct autonomous nodes across unreliable networks.

explanation.title: The network splits one action into independent outcomes
explanation.text: After the order service sends an inventory request, inventory may have processed it, not received it, or processed it while the response was lost. Do not treat order-service success as proof that checkout completed; preserve the cross-service request identity and each result.

explanation.title: Return feedback to the same business operation
explanation.text: After an inventory timeout, use the request ID to determine what happened on both sides, then choose waiting, retrying, compensating, or informing the user. Verify a normal request and an unreachable-service request after the fix; these mechanisms improve judgment and recovery but do not remove network failure.

explanation.title: Online meeting transcription is also distributed
explanation.text: The recording service may have saved the audio while the transcription service returned nothing after a network timeout. Record the saved-audio and transcription states under the same meeting ID so the system can retry transcription instead of asking the user to record again.

data.boundary: The defining feature is not a large codebase or doing things concurrently, but multiple nodes that coordinate over a network and can fail independently. Multiple threads in one process usually share process memory and are not automatically distributed; splitting services also does not automatically solve consistency, retries, or coordination.

lessonPractice.title: The order service created an order, but the inventory service timed out over the network. Which judgment fits a distributed system?

options.label: Use the request ID to inspect both services and separate completed, timed-out, and retryable steps
options.feedback: Correct. A network boundary allows partial success, so the current order state and next action require evidence from each node.

options.label: Because the order service returned success, assume inventory was definitely deducted
options.feedback: Separate service calls can end differently when the network fails; one service's success does not prove another completed.

options.label: Inspect only the order service's thread count without checking the inter-service request and response
options.feedback: Thread count cannot show whether inventory received the request, processed it, or lost the response on the network.

data.agentPrompt: Inspect the order and inventory services in the checkout flow. Keep one request ID across the call, and record sent, received, success, failure, and timeout results separately. Simulate an unreachable inventory service and state the order status, retry behavior, and how duplicate stock deduction is prevented. Verify one normal order and one inventory-timeout case with observable results from each service.

references.title: How to build reliable systems with unreliable components
